questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economics is best defined as the study of
options: how people and society choose to use scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants
how banks lend money to customers
questions.explanation: Economics studies the allocation of limited (scarce) resources to meet the unlimited wants of individuals and society.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The economic problem arises fundamentally because
options: human wants are unlimited while resources to satisfy them are limited
prices of goods are always too high
governments refuse to print enough money
banks refuse to give out loans
questions.explanation: Scarcity — the gap between limited resources and unlimited wants — is the basic economic problem faced by every society.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The act of selecting one alternative out of several competing uses for a scarce resource is called
questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce, individuals and societies must make a choice about how to allocate them among competing uses.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made is called
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost measures what is given up (the best alternative) when one option is chosen over another.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An arrangement of a consumer's wants in order of importance, from the most pressing to the least pressing, is called a
questions.explanation: A scale of preference ranks wants by urgency, helping an individual decide which wants to satisfy first given limited resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An economic system in which resources are owned and allocated mainly by private individuals through the market is called
questions.explanation: In a capitalist (free market) economy, private individuals and firms own resources, and prices set by market forces guide allocation decisions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An economic system in which resources are owned and allocated mainly by the state or government is called
questions.explanation: Under socialism, the government owns key resources and directs production and distribution through central planning rather than market forces.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An economic system that combines features of both private enterprise and government control/ownership of resources is called a
questions.explanation: A mixed economy allows both private and public ownership, blending market forces with government intervention.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An economic system in which production and distribution are guided mainly by customs and inherited practices, with little role for markets or central planning, is called a
questions.explanation: Traditional economies rely on custom, heritage, and long-established practices to decide what, how, and for whom to produce.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One advantage of a free market (capitalist) economy is that it
options: encourages efficiency and innovation through competition
removes the need for prices altogether
guarantees equal distribution of income to all citizens
questions.explanation: Competition among private firms in a free market economy tends to drive efficiency, innovation, and consumer choice.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One disadvantage of a socialist (command) economy is that it
options: may reduce individual incentive and innovation due to lack of private ownership
questions.explanation: Without private ownership and profit incentives, individuals and firms in a command economy may have less motivation to innovate or work efficiently.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The branch of economic reasoning that starts from general principles and applies them to specific situations is called
questions.explanation: Deductive reasoning moves from general economic theories/laws to explain or predict specific outcomes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The branch of economic reasoning that starts from specific observations and builds up general theories or conclusions is called
questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning derives general economic principles from patterns observed in specific real-world data.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An economic statement that describes 'what is' and can be tested against facts is called
questions.explanation: Positive economics deals with objective, factual statements that can be verified or refuted by evidence.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An economic statement that expresses an opinion about 'what ought to be' is called
questions.explanation: Normative economics involves value judgments about what economic policy or outcomes should be, rather than objective facts.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of demand states that, all things being equal,
options: demand always equals supply at every price
as the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded rises, and vice versa
as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded also rises
quantity demanded is unrelated to price
questions.explanation: The law of demand describes an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, holding other factors constant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A table showing the various quantities of a commodity that consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices is called a
questions.explanation: A demand schedule tabulates the relationship between price levels and the corresponding quantity demanded.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A graphical representation showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded is called the
questions.explanation: The demand curve plots price against quantity demanded, typically sloping downward due to the law of demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A movement along a demand curve, caused only by a change in the price of the good itself, is called a
questions.explanation: A change in quantity demanded refers strictly to movement along the same demand curve due to a price change of that good.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An entire shift of the demand curve, caused by factors other than the price of the good itself (such as income or tastes), is called a
questions.explanation: A change in demand shifts the whole curve, reflecting changes in factors like income, tastes, or the price of related goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the price of a good is called
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded changes in response to a change in a good's own price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Price elasticity of demand is calculated as
options: percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
change in total revenue divided by change in price
percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
change in supply divided by change in demand
questions.explanation: This formula measures the sensitivity of quantity demanded to price changes, expressed as a ratio of percentage changes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If a small change in price leads to a proportionately larger change in quantity demanded, demand is said to be
questions.explanation: Elastic demand means quantity demanded is highly responsive to price changes, with the percentage change in quantity exceeding the percentage change in price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If a change in price leads to a proportionately smaller change in quantity demanded, demand is said to be
questions.explanation: Inelastic demand means quantity demanded responds only slightly to price changes, common for necessities with few substitutes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in consumers' income is called
questions.explanation: Income elasticity of demand measures how quantity demanded changes as consumer income rises or falls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: For a normal good, income elasticity of demand is
options: negative, since demand falls as income rises
positive, since demand rises as income rises
questions.explanation: Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand for them increases as consumers' incomes increase.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: For an inferior good, income elasticity of demand is
options: positive, since demand rises as income rises
negative, since demand falls as income rises
questions.explanation: Inferior goods have negative income elasticity because consumers buy less of them as their incomes rise, switching to better alternatives.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The responsiveness of the quantity demanded of one good to a change in the price of another good is called
questions.explanation: Cross elasticity of demand measures how the quantity demanded of one good changes when the price of a related good changes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: For two goods that are complements (such as bread and butter), cross elasticity of demand is
questions.explanation: Complementary goods have negative cross elasticity: a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other, since they are used together.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of supply states that, all things being equal,
options: as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied falls
as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied also rises, and vice versa
questions.explanation: The law of supply describes a direct (positive) relationship between price and quantity supplied, holding other factors constant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A table showing the various quantities of a commodity that producers are willing to sell at different prices is called a
questions.explanation: A supply schedule tabulates the relationship between price levels and the corresponding quantity supplied.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An entire shift of the supply curve, caused by factors other than price (such as production costs or technology), is called a
questions.explanation: A change in supply shifts the whole curve, reflecting factors like input costs, technology, or the number of producers in the market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the price of a good is called
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of supply measures how quantity supplied responds to changes in the good's own price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The point at which the quantity demanded of a good exactly equals the quantity supplied is called
questions.explanation: Market equilibrium occurs where the demand and supply curves intersect, determining the equilibrium price and quantity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A situation where the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied at a given price is called a
questions.explanation: A shortage occurs when consumers wish to buy more than producers supply at the prevailing price, pushing price up toward equilibrium.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A legally imposed price above which a commodity may not be sold, aimed at protecting producers, is called a
questions.explanation: A price floor (minimum price) is set above the equilibrium price to guarantee producers a certain return, often creating a persistent surplus.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A legally imposed price above which a commodity may not be sold, aimed at protecting consumers, is called a
questions.explanation: A price ceiling (maximum price) is set below the equilibrium price to keep essential goods affordable, but it often creates a shortage.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The four traditional factors of production are
questions.explanation: Economics identifies land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship as the basic resources combined to produce goods and services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The reward paid to the factor of production 'land' is called
questions.explanation: Rent is the payment made for the use of land and other natural resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The reward paid to the factor of production 'labour' is called
questions.explanation: Wages (or salaries) are payments made to workers for their labour services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The reward paid to the factor of production 'capital' is called
questions.explanation: Interest is the payment made for the use of capital, such as money borrowed or invested.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The reward paid to the factor of production 'entrepreneur' is called
questions.explanation: Profit is the reward an entrepreneur earns for organising other factors of production and bearing business risk.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of diminishing returns states that as more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor,
options: output will eventually increase at a decreasing rate
output will always increase at a constant rate
questions.explanation: The law of diminishing returns applies in the short run, where adding more of a variable input to fixed inputs eventually yields smaller and smaller additions to output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Breaking down a production process into separate, specialised tasks performed by different workers is called
questions.explanation: Division of labour splits work into specialised tasks, which can raise efficiency and productivity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One advantage of division of labour is that it
options: guarantees full employment in an economy
eliminates the need for factors of production
increases efficiency and output through specialisation
questions.explanation: By allowing workers to focus on tasks they are skilled at, division of labour tends to raise overall productivity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent, are called
questions.explanation: Fixed costs remain constant regardless of how much (or little) is produced in the short run.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Costs that change directly with the level of output, such as raw materials, are called
questions.explanation: Variable costs rise and fall with the quantity of output produced, unlike fixed costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Total cost is calculated as
questions.explanation: Total cost combines both the constant fixed costs and the output-dependent variable costs of production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The cost of producing one additional unit of output is called
questions.explanation: Marginal cost measures the extra cost incurred from producing one more unit of a good.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Total cost divided by the quantity of output produced gives the
questions.explanation: Average (total) cost is the cost per unit of output, found by dividing total cost by quantity produced.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The total amount of money a firm receives from selling its output is called
questions.explanation: Total revenue equals the price per unit multiplied by the quantity of units sold.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The additional revenue earned from selling one more unit of output is called
questions.explanation: Marginal revenue measures the change in total revenue resulting from selling one extra unit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A market structure in which there are many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, and free entry and exit is called
questions.explanation: Perfect competition is characterised by many small firms selling identical products, with no single firm able to influence market price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Under perfect competition, an individual firm is described as a
questions.explanation: Since firms in perfect competition are small relative to the market and sell identical goods, they must accept the market-determined price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A market structure in which a single firm is the sole supplier of a good or service, with no close substitutes, is called a
questions.explanation: A monopoly exists when one firm dominates the entire market for a product with no close substitutes available.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A market structure with many firms selling similar but slightly differentiated products is called
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition features many sellers offering differentiated products (through branding, quality, etc.), giving each some pricing power.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A market structure dominated by a small number of large firms, often interdependent in their pricing and output decisions, is called
questions.explanation: In an oligopoly, a few large firms dominate the market, and each firm's decisions significantly affect and are affected by its rivals.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period is called
questions.explanation: GDP measures output produced within a country's geographical boundaries, regardless of who owns the resources used.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The total monetary value of goods and services produced by a country's nationals, both at home and abroad, is called
questions.explanation: GNP measures output produced by a country's citizens and businesses regardless of location, unlike GDP which is location-based.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: GNP minus depreciation (capital consumption allowance) gives the
questions.explanation: NNP adjusts GNP for the wear and tear (depreciation) of capital equipment used in production during the period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The income actually received by individuals before personal taxes are deducted is called
questions.explanation: Personal income is the total income received by households from all sources, before personal income tax is deducted.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Personal Income minus personal income taxes gives
questions.explanation: Disposable income is what individuals actually have available to spend or save after taxes have been deducted.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The method of measuring national income by adding up all incomes earned by factors of production is called the
questions.explanation: The income approach sums wages, rent, interest, and profit earned by all factors of production in the economy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The method of measuring national income by adding up all spending on final goods and services is called the
questions.explanation: The expenditure approach sums consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports to measure national income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The method of measuring national income by adding up the value of output produced by all sectors of the economy is called the
questions.explanation: The output approach totals the value added by each industry or sector to avoid double-counting intermediate goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Counting the value of a good more than once at different stages of production when measuring national income is called the problem of
questions.explanation: Double counting inflates national income figures by including the value of intermediate goods multiple times; using value-added avoids this.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Money can be best described as
options: an asset that always loses its value over time
any object used only for decoration
a good that cannot be exchanged for other goods
anything generally acceptable as a medium of exchange
questions.explanation: Money serves as a widely accepted medium of exchange, facilitating trade without requiring a double coincidence of wants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The function of money that allows it to be used to buy goods and services directly is called
questions.explanation: As a medium of exchange, money is accepted in transactions for goods and services, replacing the need for barter.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The function of money that allows prices of different goods to be compared using a common measure is called
questions.explanation: As a unit of account, money provides a common standard for expressing and comparing the value of different goods and services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The function of money that allows wealth to be saved and used at a later date is called
questions.explanation: Money serves as a store of value, allowing purchasing power to be preserved over time (though inflation can erode this).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The desire to hold money for day-to-day transactions such as buying food and paying bills is called the
questions.explanation: The transactionary motive reflects the need to hold cash to cover routine, everyday spending.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The desire to hold money to meet unforeseen or emergency expenses is called the
questions.explanation: The precautionary motive reflects holding extra cash as a buffer against unexpected needs or emergencies.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The desire to hold money in order to take advantage of expected future changes in interest rates or asset prices is called the
questions.explanation: The speculative motive involves holding money to invest later when conditions (such as interest rates or prices) become more favourable.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A bank that accepts deposits from the public and grants short- to medium-term loans is called a
questions.explanation: Commercial banks are the primary retail banks that handle deposits, withdrawals, and lending for individuals and businesses.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The bank responsible for issuing a country's currency and controlling the overall money supply is the
questions.explanation: The central bank has the sole authority to issue legal tender currency and implement monetary policy for the whole economy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Central bank actions aimed at controlling the money supply and interest rates to influence the economy are called
questions.explanation: Monetary policy involves tools like interest rates and open market operations, used by the central bank to manage money supply and economic activity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A persistent, sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services in an economy is called
questions.explanation: Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money as prices rise generally across the economy over time.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Inflation caused by too much money chasing too few goods, i.e., excess aggregate demand, is called
questions.explanation: Demand-pull inflation arises when total demand in the economy outstrips the available supply of goods and services, driving prices up.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Inflation caused by rising production costs, such as wages or raw material prices, being passed on to consumers is called
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation occurs when increased costs of production lead firms to raise prices to maintain profit margins.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Government revenue collected directly from individuals and businesses, such as personal income tax and company tax, is called
questions.explanation: Direct taxes are levied directly on the income or wealth of individuals and firms and cannot easily be shifted to another party.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Government revenue collected on goods and services, such as excise duty and import duty, is called
questions.explanation: Indirect taxes are levied on goods and services and can often be passed on, at least in part, from sellers to buyers through prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The economic principle stating that a tax should be proportional to a taxpayer's ability to pay is the canon of
questions.explanation: The canon of equity requires that taxes be fair, generally taking more from those with a greater capacity to pay.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The economic principle stating that the amount, time, and manner of tax payment should be clear to the taxpayer is the canon of
questions.explanation: The canon of certainty requires that taxpayers know exactly how much tax to pay, when, and how, without arbitrary changes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The economic principle stating that taxes should be collected in a manner and at a time convenient to the taxpayer is the canon of
questions.explanation: The canon of convenience ensures the method and timing of tax collection are easy and suitable for the taxpayer, such as deducting tax at source.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The economic principle stating that the cost of collecting a tax should be low relative to the revenue it generates is the canon of
questions.explanation: The canon of economy requires that the administrative cost of collecting a tax should not be excessive compared to the revenue raised.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A budget in which planned government expenditure exceeds planned government revenue is called a
questions.explanation: A deficit budget occurs when a government plans to spend more than it expects to collect in revenue, requiring borrowing to cover the gap.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A budget in which planned government revenue exceeds planned government expenditure is called a
questions.explanation: A surplus budget occurs when a government expects to collect more revenue than it plans to spend.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A budget in which planned government revenue exactly equals planned government expenditure is called a
questions.explanation: A balanced budget occurs when total planned revenue equals total planned expenditure, with neither a surplus nor a deficit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The theory stating that a country should specialise in producing goods it can make relatively more efficiently than others, and trade for the rest, is called the theory of
questions.explanation: The theory of comparative advantage shows that countries gain from trade by specialising in goods they produce at a relatively lower opportunity cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The ratio of the prices a country receives for its exports to the prices it pays for its imports is called the
questions.explanation: Terms of trade compare export prices to import prices, indicating how much a country can import for a given quantity of exports.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Government policy of restricting imports through tariffs, quotas, or other barriers to shield domestic industries from foreign competition is called
questions.explanation: Protectionism uses trade barriers to protect local producers from cheaper or more competitive foreign goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A policy that allows goods and services to move between countries without tariffs, quotas, or other restrictions is called
questions.explanation: Free trade removes barriers to international trade, allowing goods and services to be exchanged based purely on market forces.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A deliberate reduction in the official value of a country's currency in terms of other currencies is called
questions.explanation: Devaluation lowers a currency's official exchange rate, typically to make exports cheaper and imports more expensive.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A deliberate increase in the official value of a country's currency in terms of other currencies is called
questions.explanation: Revaluation raises a currency's official exchange rate, typically making exports more expensive and imports cheaper.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economic growth is best defined as
options: an increase in a country's population only
a sustained increase in a country's real output (real GDP) over time
a rise in the general price level
a fall in the unemployment rate only
questions.explanation: Economic growth measures the expansion of an economy's productive capacity and output over a sustained period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economic development is a broader concept than economic growth because it also includes
options: only the increase in a country's population
only the increase in a country's GDP
only the value of a country's exports
improvements in living standards, health, education, and general welfare
questions.explanation: Economic development covers qualitative improvements in well-being (health, education, equality) beyond just growth in output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A common characteristic of most developing countries is
options: heavy dependence on the export of primary (agricultural or mineral) products
questions.explanation: Many developing economies rely significantly on exporting raw agricultural or mineral commodities rather than finished manufactured goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The regional body established mainly to promote economic integration and free movement of goods and people among West African states is
options: the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was established to promote economic cooperation, free trade, and integration among West African countries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The international financial institution that primarily provides short-term financial assistance to countries facing balance of payments problems is the
questions.explanation: The IMF offers financial support and policy advice to member countries experiencing balance of payments difficulties.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The international financial institution that primarily provides long-term loans for development and reconstruction projects is the
questions.explanation: The World Bank funds long-term development projects such as infrastructure, education, and health, unlike the IMF's shorter-term focus.
